This is a coaching and programming philosophy question, not a programme change — so I'll step outside the DSL to answer it directly.

Leave the cue alone in a peaking block.

Here is the reasoning:

Three weeks out is not the time to introduce or reinforce a technical change. Even a beneficial cue, drilled hard now, can make a movement feel unfamiliar under maximal load on meet day. The nervous system needs to express a pattern it already owns, not one it is still consolidating.

If the scapular retraction cue is already part of her grooved pattern from the accumulation block, it will show up automatically — you do not need to drill it. If it is a new correction she has been experimenting with, drilling it now risks her hitting her opener and thinking about her shoulder blades instead of just pressing.

What to do instead:

One simple, familiar, confidence-building cue per lift on meet day. For bench that is usually something like "big air, tight back, drive the bar" — whatever she has used successfully for months, not whatever she has been working on recently.

After the meet, in the first week of the next training block, revisit the retraction cue properly. Film her, assess whether it is actually improving her shelf and leg drive transfer, and build it in from the start of accumulation so it has 12 weeks to become automatic before the next peak.

The rule in a peaking block is: trust the training, reduce the noise.

Again, this is coaching guidance rather than a programme output, so stepping outside the DSL.

---

MORNING TIMELINE — MEET DAY

This assumes a 10:00am first attempt. Adjust all times proportionally if her flight is later.

---

6:00am — Wake and eat
Small, familiar meal. Nothing new. Carbohydrates she has eaten before, moderate protein, low fat and fibre to avoid GI issues. Coffee if she normally has it — not the time to experiment either way.

---

7:00am — Arrive at venue
Weigh in if same-day. Get rack height and attempt numbers confirmed early. Walk the floor, find the warm-up room, locate the attempt board and the caller.

---

8:00am — First movement
Ten minutes of easy walking or light cycling if a bike is available in the warm-up room. RPE 2. The goal is blood flow and body temperature, not activation. Keep it genuinely easy.

---

8:20am — General warm-up
Cat-cow, hip circles, leg swings, shoulder circles, thoracic rotation. Five to eight minutes. Nothing that creates fatigue.

---

8:35am — Squat warm-up begins
A typical ladder for an intermediate lifter with, say, a 120kg opener:

- Bar only — 2x5, relaxed, groove the pattern
- 50kg — 2x3
- 70kg — 2x2
- 85kg — 1x2
- 100kg — 1x1
- 110kg — 1x1
- Last warm-up single approximately 8 to 10 minutes before she walks out for attempt one

The last warm-up should be around 92 to 95 percent of her opener — heavy enough to feel real, light enough that she racks it thinking that was easy.

---

TIMING RULE
Work backwards from her first attempt. The last warm-up single should finish with one full rest interval before she is called. For most meets that means she needs to know roughly what attempt number she is and how fast the flight is moving. Assign someone — a handler or you — to watch the board and manage her timing. She should not be doing this herself.

---

OPENERS
Opener should be a guaranteed lift. Something she could triple on a bad day. Typically 90 to 92 percent of her current training max. The meet is won on second and third attempts — the opener just gets her on the board and settles her nerves.

---

BENCH AND DEADLIFT
Same ladder logic, compressed slightly because she will have less time between flights. Bench warm-ups can start later since upper body recovers faster. Deadlift warm-ups should be conservative — pulls are taxing and she will already have squatted. Fewer singles, more rest.

---

ONE THING TO TELL HER
The warm-up room will feel chaotic. Bars will be taken, timing will slip, people will be loud. Brief her on this now so it is not a surprise. The plan is the anchor. Stick to the ladder, trust the numbers, ignore everything else.

Stepping outside the DSL — this is nutrition guidance, not a programme output.

---

48 HOURS OUT — NUTRITION PROTOCOL

The goal is liver and muscle glycogen saturation, stable hydration, and no GI surprises on the platform. Nothing radical. This is not a bodybuilding peak — she is not cutting water or sodium. She just needs to be full, hydrated, and comfortable.

---

CARBOHYDRATES

Start a moderate carbohydrate increase 48 hours out. Not a dramatic load — her glycogen is already reasonably stocked from training. The goal is topping off, not stuffing.

Target roughly 5 to 7 grams of carbohydrate per kilogram of bodyweight across the two days. For a 70kg athlete that is 350 to 490 grams per day. Spread across four to five meals.

Sources should be familiar, low fibre, and easy to digest. White rice, white pasta, white bread, oats, banana, fruit juice, sports drinks. This is not the time for brown rice, legumes, cruciferous vegetables, or anything that causes bloating or unpredictable digestion.

Reduce fat intake slightly across these two days — fat slows gastric emptying and competes with carbohydrate storage. Keep protein moderate and consistent with what she normally eats.

---

FLUIDS

She should be drinking consistently across both days, not aggressively loading water in one sitting. Pale yellow urine is the target. Dark urine means she is behind. Clear urine means she has overdone it and may be diluting electrolytes.

A practical target is around 35 to 45ml per kilogram of bodyweight per day from all fluid sources. Again for a 70kg athlete that is roughly 2.5 to 3 litres across the day including food moisture.

Avoid alcohol entirely. Avoid excessive caffeine beyond her normal intake.

---

SODIUM

Do not restrict sodium. This is a common mistake borrowed from weight-cut protocols that do not apply here. She is not cutting weight. Normal dietary sodium across both days helps her retain the fluid she is drinking and supports nerve and muscle function.

If anything, slightly salting meals is fine and beneficial. Sports drinks with electrolytes during the day are useful, particularly if she tends to sweat a lot or has been training in a warm environment.

---

MEET MORNING

Meal two to three hours before lifting. Familiar food. Moderate carbohydrates, moderate protein, low fat, low fibre. Something like white rice and eggs, toast with peanut butter and banana, or oats with fruit. Whatever she has eaten before early morning training sessions without issue.

Bring food and drinks to the meet. Between flights she should be sipping fluids and eating small carbohydrate snacks — rice cakes, white bread, fruit, gels, sports drink. She will be at the venue for several hours and glycogen will deplete across the day.

---

ONE THING TO AVOID

A big unfamiliar meal the night before because she is nervous and wants to feel prepared. This is how athletes end up on the platform feeling bloated and sluggish. Same foods she knows. Same portions she is used to. Just slightly more carbohydrate than a normal training day.
